lead: An SI engine burns a premixed fuel–air charge after a spark. Combustion runs in three stages: ignition lag, flame propagation and afterburning. Ignition lag is the short delay before a flame kernel grows enough to raise pressure. Flame propagation is the thin flame front sweeping the unburnt mixture. Afterburning finishes the last gas near the walls. Mechanics read these stages on the pressure–crank angle trace to judge spark timing and cyclic variation.
prereq: You need: the four-stroke SI working principle from Unit 1 and spark timing from Unit 2.

blocks.text: Combustion starts at the spark plug. The spark leaves a small flame kernel, but the kernel needs time to become self-sustaining. That delay is ignition lag. In a normal engine it is about 0.001 s to 0.002 s. Some syllabi call it the preparation phase: the kernel grows, radical species build up and local temperature rises. Pressure barely changes during most of this delay. The stage ends when pressure first rises above the motoring curve.

Flame propagation follows. A thin flame front, a reaction zone perhaps a millimetre thick, moves into the unburnt mixture. Behind it is burnt gas; ahead is fresh charge. The front area and flame speed decide how fast fresh charge is consumed. Cylinder pressure rises steeply. The stage ends when the flame has swept the main chamber, usually a few tens of crank degrees after top dead centre (TDC).

Afterburning is the last stage. Unburnt gas trapped in crevices, near the cold wall or in a lean pocket burns slowly. Pressure falls as the piston moves down. Oxidation of CO and hydrocarbons continues into the expansion stroke. It adds little useful work but affects emissions.
Each stage has a crank-angle width, not a fixed time. At higher speed the same milliseconds cover more degrees. The spark must be advanced so that the steep pressure rise happens near TDC.

The pressure–crank angle trace plots cylinder pressure p against crank angle θ. θ is measured from TDC; negative θ is before TDC. The motoring curve is the pressure with fuel but no ignition. The spark marker sits at spark timing. The trace leaves the motoring curve at the end of ignition lag; that knee is the practical end of lag.

During flame propagation the trace climbs steeply to peak pressure. Peak pressure normally occurs near 10° to 15° after TDC. Too early a peak means over-advanced spark; too late means retarded spark. The main flame sweep ends near 40° to 45° after TDC in many engines. The remaining slow fall is afterburning.

blocks.where: θ is crank angle in degrees; N is engine speed in rev/min; t is time in seconds; t<sub>ms</sub> is the same time in milliseconds.

blocks.text: At 3000 rpm, 1 ms is 18° CA. The same 1.5 ms lag is 27° at 3000 rpm but 9° at 1000 rpm.

Cyclic variation is normal: the same settings give slightly different traces cycle to cycle. Peak pressure and peak angle scatter. Heavy scatter points to a weak flame kernel, poor mixture preparation or too lean a charge. It is tracked by the coefficient of variation of indicated mean effective pressure, COV of IMEP.

The three-stage picture sets the language for the rest of the unit. Flame speed and mass burning rate control the slope of the pressure rise; see 3.2. If the end gas ahead of the flame autoignites, the trace shows a pressure spike and knock; see 3.3. Ignition lag is not flame propagation: lag is delay before burning, propagation is the burning wave.

If ignition lag is too long, the spark needs more advance. If flame propagation is slow, peak pressure arrives late and work falls. If afterburning is heavy, exhaust temperature and unburnt hydrocarbons rise. These three checks are the first things to look at when an engine loses power or knocks. Chamber shape and air motion change flame speed; see 3.7 and 3.8.

figure.caption: The spark fires at 15° before TDC. Pressure first rises at 12° after TDC, the main flame sweep ends at 42°, and the slow afterburning tail ends at 62°.

spec.aria: Timeline from 15 degrees before top dead centre to 62 degrees after top dead centre: ignition lag ends at 12 degrees after TDC, flame propagation ends at 42 degrees, and afterburning ends at 62 degrees.

examples.question: A spark fires at 15° bTDC. Ignition lag is 1.5 ms. The engine runs at 3000 rpm. Find the ignition lag in crank degrees and the crank angle where the pressure starts to rise (end of ignition lag). Then mark flame propagation of 30° CA and afterburning of 20° CA on a crank-angle timeline.
steps: Engine speed N = 3000 rpm. Time for one revolution = 60 / 3000 = 0.020 s = 20 ms.
Ignition lag in crank degrees = 1.5 ms × 18 °CA/ms = 27° CA.
Spark at 15° bTDC is −15° from TDC. End of lag = −15° + 27° = +12° aTDC.
examples.answer: Ignition lag is 27° CA; it ends at 12° aTDC; flame propagation ends at 42° aTDC; afterburning ends at 62° aTDC.
examples.check:
rpm = 3000.0
lag_ms = 1.5
spark_deg = -15.0
ms_per_rev = 60000.0 / rpm
deg_per_ms = 360.0 / ms_per_rev
lag_deg = lag_ms * deg_per_ms
end_lag = spark_deg + lag_deg
flame_end = end_lag + 30.0
after_end = flame_end + 20.0
print(lag_deg)
print(end_lag)
print(flame_end)
print(after_end)

traps: Ignition lag ends at the first pressure rise above the motoring curve, not when the flame reaches the cylinder wall.
Ignition lag is delay before burning; flame propagation is the burning wave. Do not use the two terms for the same stage.
Crank degrees and milliseconds are different units. A 1.5 ms lag is 27° CA at 3000 rpm but only 9° CA at 1000 rpm.
Spark advance is a setting before TDC; ignition lag is the delay after the spark. Advancing the spark does not shorten the chemical lag in milliseconds.
Afterburning is the slow oxidation tail, not the main flame sweep. Peak pressure belongs to the end of flame propagation, not to afterburning.

quiz.q: List the three stages of combustion in an SI engine in order.
Why does a fixed ignition lag in milliseconds cover more crank degrees at higher engine speed?
quiz.a: Crank degrees θ = 6 N t. For the same t, θ rises in proportion to engine speed N, so the spark timing must be adjusted.

quiz.q: At 2000 rpm, ignition lag is 1.2 ms and the spark fires at 12° bTDC. Find the lag in crank degrees and the crank angle where pressure starts to rise.
quiz.a: One revolution takes 60/2000 = 0.030 s = 30 ms. Degrees per ms = 360/30 = 12 °CA/ms. Lag = 1.2 × 12 = 14.4° CA. End of lag = −12° + 14.4° = 2.4° aTDC. Pressure starts to rise at 2.4° aTDC.

quiz.q: A pressure–crank angle trace leaves the motoring curve at 8° aTDC and reaches peak pressure at 20° aTDC. Which stage ends at 8°? What does the late peak suggest?
quiz.a: Ignition lag ends at 8° aTDC. A peak at 20° aTDC is late; it suggests retarded spark or slow flame propagation, so more spark advance or better mixture preparation may be needed.

quiz.q: Give the typical ignition lag range for a normal SI engine.
Why is the flame front called a thin reaction zone?
quiz.a: The chemical reaction is concentrated in a narrow layer between burnt gas and unburnt charge. The whole charge does not burn at once; the thin front moves through it.

quiz.q: How does cyclic variation appear on pressure traces, and why use COV of IMEP?
quiz.a: Peak pressure and its crank angle scatter from cycle to cycle. The coefficient of variation of indicated mean effective pressure, COV of IMEP, puts a number on that scatter. High COV means unstable combustion and poor driveability.

quiz.q: At 4000 rpm, ignition lag is 1.0 ms and the spark fires at 20° bTDC. Find the lag in crank degrees and the crank angle where pressure starts to rise.
quiz.a: One revolution takes 60/4000 = 0.015 s = 15 ms. Degrees per ms = 360/15 = 24 °CA/ms. Lag = 1.0 × 24 = 24° CA. End of lag = −20° + 24° = 4° aTDC. Pressure starts to rise at 4° aTDC.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern SI engines use statistical ignition timing control and cylinder-pressure or ion-current feedback to hold the 50% mass-burned point near 8–10° aTDC. High-speed optical engines with laser diagnostics show the flame kernel wrinkling and the flame front thickness directly. Researchers tune flame speed with charge motion, stratification and dilution (lean burn or exhaust gas recirculation) to shorten propagation. Search terms: mass fraction burned, Wiebe function, flame kernel growth, cycle-to-cycle variation, COV of IMEP.
